newsitem.title: FRANCE: France's future ex-premier fights on for victory.
newsitem.headline: France's future ex-premier fights on for victory.

text.p: France's future ex-prime minister threw his body and soul into campaigning on Tuesday for a centre-right victory in next Sunday's cliffhanger election runoff a day after sacrificing his own job.

The morning after he announced he would resign whatever the outcome of the parliamentary runoff, Alain Juppe deserted his Matignon office to hit the campaign trail in the southern town of Avignon, showing an unsuspected streak of self-criticism.

Juppe urged voters to give fellow Gaullist President Jacques Chirac a majority and not hand France back to "the Mitterrand generation" by electing a Socialist-led government in Sunday's decisive second round.
He would not comment on whom Chirac might appoint to replace him if the coalition snatches victory from the jaws of defeat.

"As we saw in the 1995 presidential campaign, his diagnosis was right. Maybe he has suffered from errors in the last two years, the backlash of errors which I may have made, but now is the time to give him the means to start a new chapter with new men," the outgoing premier said.

Juppe, 51, fell on his sword on Monday less than 24 hours after the centre-right suffered a stinging rebuff in the first round of voting, outpolled by more than four points by the combined left-wing opposition.

Polling institutes said rejection of Juppe's personality and record was a key factor. They projected that the left would win a narrow overall majority in the National Assembly if the same voting pattern were repeated on Sunday.
The outgoing premier showed his emotions, his voice wavering as he thanked Gaullist party activists whose support, he said, had been precious "at difficult moments such as this".
He made a special appeal to doctors, many of whom have been alienated from the Gaullists by his overhaul of France's costly public health and social security system.

"I know many doctors wanted to punish the government on the first round, as they told us," Juppe said. "I continue to think our reform was necessary, inevitable and unavoidable...but nothing is engraved in stone."
The medical profession was particularly angered by measures to fine doctors collectively if health spending exceeds pre-set targets in their region.

"I ask simply...is it better to have this reform implemented intelligently and understandingly by a coalition that respects and is committed to the principles of liberal medicine, or by another majority that does not have the same aims and would surely push our system towards state bureaucracy?" Juppe said.

His jibe against the generation brought to power by the late president Francois Mitterrand was aimed directly at Avignon, where Gaullist mayor Marie-Josee Roig faces a strong challenge from former Socialist European affairs minister Elisabeth Guigou, a one-time adviser to Mitterrand.
"When voting out of discontent, be careful not to do the opposite of what you really want for yourself and for France," Juppe said. "The return to socialism is the opposite of change."
